title: Fluorine in biology
wikitext:
{{Short description|none}}
[[File:PET-MIPS-anim.gif|thumb|PET scan using fluorine-18|alt=A rotating, transparent image of a human figure with targeted organs highlighted]]

[[Fluorine]] may interact with biological systems in the form of fluorine-containing compounds. Though elemental fluorine (F<sub>2</sub>) is very rare in everyday life, fluorine-containing compounds such as [[fluorite]] occur naturally as minerals. Naturally occurring [[organofluorine]] compounds are extremely rare. Man-made fluoride compounds are common and are used in medicines, pesticides, and materials. Twenty percent of all commercialized pharmaceuticals contain fluorine, including [[Lipitor]] and [[Prozac]].<ref name=Ullmann>G. Siegemund, W. Schwertfeger, A. Feiring, B. Smart, F. Behr, H. Vogel, B. McKusick "Fluorine Compounds, Organic" in "Ullmann's Encyclopedia of Industrial Chemistry" 2005, Wiley-VCH, Weinheim. {{doi|10.1002/14356007.a11_349}}</ref><ref name=Aigueperse>{{citation | first1 = Jean | last1 = Aigueperse | first2 = Paul | last2 = Mollard | first3 = Didier | last3 = Devilliers | first4= Marius | last4 = Chemla | first5 =  Robert | last5 = Faron | first6 = Renée | last6 = Romano | first7 = Jean Pierre | last7 = Cuer | contribution = Fluorine Compounds, Inorganic | editor-last = Ullmann | title = Encyclopedia of Industrial Chemistry | year = 2005 | publisher = Wiley-VCH | place = Weinheim|doi = 10.1002/14356007.a11_307| isbn = 978-3527306732 }}</ref> In many contexts, fluorine-containing compounds are harmless or even beneficial to living organisms; in others, they are [[fluoride toxicity|toxic]].

Aside from their use in medicine, man-made fluorinated compounds have also played a role in several noteworthy environmental concerns. [[Chlorofluorocarbons]] (CFCs), once major components of numerous commercial aerosol products, have proven damaging to Earth's [[ozone layer]] and resulted in the wide-reaching [[Montreal Protocol]]; though in truth the [[chlorine]] in CFCs is the destructive actor, fluorine is an important part of these molecules because it makes them very stable and long-lived. Similarly, the stability of many [[organofluorine compound]]s has raised the issue of [[Persistent organic pollutant|biopersistence]]. Long-lived molecules from waterproofing sprays, for example [[PFOA]] and [[PFOS]], are found worldwide in the tissues of wildlife and humans, including newborn children.

Fluorine biology is also relevant to a number of cutting-edge technologies. PFCs ([[perfluorocarbons]]) are capable of holding enough oxygen to support human [[liquid breathing]]. Organofluorine in the form of its radioisotope [[Fluorine-18|<sup>18</sup>F]] is also at the heart of a modern medical imaging technique known as [[positron emission tomography]] (PET). A PET scan produces three-dimensional colored images of parts of the body that use a lot of sugar, particularly the brain or tumors.

==Dental care==
{{Main|Fluoride therapy|Water fluoridation}}
Since the mid-20th century, it has been discerned from population studies (though incompletely understood) that fluoride reduces [[tooth decay]]. Initially, researchers hypothesized that fluoride helped by converting [[tooth enamel]] from the more acid-soluble mineral [[hydroxyapatite]] to the less acid-soluble mineral fluorapatite. However, more recent studies showed no difference in the frequency of [[caries]] (cavities) between teeth that were pre-fluoridated to different degrees. Current thinking is that fluoride prevents cavities primarily by helping teeth that are in the very early stages of tooth decay.<ref name=Pizzo/>

[[File:US Navy 090526-F-1333S-023 A service member embarked aboard the Military Sealift Command hospital ship USNS Comfort (T-AH 20) gives a Fluoride treatment to a patient during a Continuing Promise 2009 medical civil service projec.jpg|thumb|alt=white man holding plastic tray with brown goop in it and sticking a small stick into a black boy's open mouth|Topical fluoride treatment in Panama]]
When teeth begin to decay from the acid produced by sugar-consuming bacteria, [[calcium]] is lost (''demineralization''). However, teeth have a limited ability to recover calcium if decay is not too far advanced (''remineralization''). Fluoride appears to reduce demineralization and increase remineralization. Also, there is some evidence that fluoride interferes with the bacteria that consume sugars in the mouth and make tooth-destroying acids.<ref name=Pizzo/> In any case, it is only the fluoride that is directly present in the mouth ([[topical medication|topical treatment]]) that prevents cavities; fluoride ions that are swallowed do not benefit the teeth.<ref name=Pizzo>{{cite journal |author1=Pizzo G. |author2=Piscopo, M. R. |author3=Pizzo, I. |author4=Giuliana, G. |title= Community water fluoridation and caries prevention: a critical review |journal= Clinical Oral Investigation |volume=11 |issue=3 |pages=189–193 |year=2007 |pmid=17333303 |doi=10.1007/s00784-007-0111-6|s2cid=13189520 |url=http://www.newmediaexplorer.org/chris/Pizzo-2007.pdf}}</ref>

[[Water fluoridation]] is the controlled addition of fluoride to a [[public water supply]] in an effort to reduce tooth decay in people who drink the water.<ref>{{cite journal |title= Recommendations for using fluoride to prevent and control dental caries in the United States |author= Centers for Disease Control and Prevention |journal= MMWR Recommendations and Reports |volume=50 |issue=RR–14 |pages=1–42 |year=2001 |pmid=11521913 |url=http://cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/rr5014a1.htm}}</ref> Its use began in the 1940s, following studies of children in a region where water is naturally fluoridated. It is now used widely in public water systems in the United States and some other parts of the world, such that about two-thirds of the U.S. population is exposed to fluoridated water supplies<ref name=Ripa>{{cite journal |author= Ripa, L. W. |url=http://aaphd.org/docs/position%20papers/A%20Half-Century%20of%20Community%20Water1993.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090304021822/http://aaphd.org/docs/position%20papers/A%20Half-Century%20of%20Community%20Water1993.pdf |archive-date=2009-03-04 |title= A half-century of community water fluoridation in the United States: review and commentary |journal= Journal of Public Health Dentistry |volume=53 |issue=1 |pages=17–44 |year=1993 |pmid=8474047 |doi= 10.1111/j.1752-7325.1993.tb02666.x}}</ref> and about 5.7% of people worldwide.<ref name=Cheng2007>{{cite journal |author1=Cheng, K. K. |author2=Chalmers, I. |author3=Sheldon, T. A. |title=Adding fluoride to water supplies |url=http://www.appgaf.org.uk/data/433-water-fluoridation.pdf |journal=BMJ |volume=335 |issue=7622 |pages=699–702 |year=2007 |pmid=17916854 |pmc=2001050 |doi=10.1136/bmj.39318.562951.BE |access-date=2013-05-12 |archive-date=2019-12-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191209235112/http://www.appgaf.org.uk/data/433-water-fluoridation.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Although the best available evidence shows no association with adverse effects other than fluorosis ([[dental fluorosis|dental]] and, in worse cases, [[skeletal fluorosis|skeletal]]), most of which is mild,<ref>{{cite book|isbn=9789350252161 |year=2011 |title=A textbook of public health dentistry|author= Marya, C. M.|page=343|publisher=JP Medical Limited}}</ref> water fluoridation has been contentious for ethical, safety, and efficacy reasons,<ref name=Cheng2007/> and [[opposition to water fluoridation]] exists despite its widespread support by [[public health]] organizations.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Armfield|first=J. M.|title= When public action undermines public health: A critical examination of antifluoridationist literature |journal= Australia and New Zealand Health Policy |volume=4 |article-number=25 |year=2007 |pmid=18067684 |pmc=2222595 |doi=10.1186/1743-8462-4-25|issue=1 |doi-access=free }}</ref> The benefits of water fluoridation have lessened recently, presumably because of the availability of fluoride in other forms, but are still measurable, particularly for low-income groups.<ref name="Dental caries"/> [[Systematic review]]s in 2000 and 2007 showed significant reduction of cavities in children exposed to water fluoridation.<ref name=NHMRC>{{cite web |url=http://www.nhmrc.gov.au/_files_nhmrc/publications/attachments/eh41_1.pdf |access-date=24 February 2009 |year=2007 |title=A systematic review of the efficacy and safety of fluoridation |author=National Health and Medical Research Council (Australia) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120113043215/http://www.nhmrc.gov.au/_files_nhmrc/publications/attachments/eh41_1.pdf |archive-date=13 January 2012 |url-status=dead }} Summary: {{cite journal |author= Yeung, C. A. |title= A systematic review of the efficacy and safety of fluoridation |journal= Evidence-Based Dentistry |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=39–43 |year=2008 |pmid=18584000 |doi=10.1038/sj.ebd.6400578 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

[[Sodium fluoride]], [[tin(II) fluoride|tin difluoride]], and, most commonly, [[sodium monofluorophosphate]], are used in [[toothpaste]]. In 1955, the first fluoride toothpaste was introduced in the United States. Now, almost all toothpaste in developed countries is fluoridated. For example, 95% of European toothpaste contains fluoride.<ref name="Dental caries">{{cite book|title=Dental caries: The disease and its clinical management|year=2008|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-1-4051-3889-5|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fZfXWhSmG1UC&pg=PA518|author=Fejerskov, Ole|author2=Kidd, Edwina|page=518}}</ref> Gels and foams are often advised for special patient groups, particularly those undergoing radiation therapy to the head (cancer patients). The patient receives a four-minute application of a high amount of fluoride. Varnishes, which can be more quickly applied, exist and perform a similar function. Fluoride is also often present in prescription and non-prescription [[mouthwash]]es and is a trace component of foods manufactured using fluoridated water supplies.<ref name="Crest continuing ed">{{cite web|last=Cracher |first=Connie Myers |title=Current concepts in preventive dentistry |url=http://www.dentalcare.com/media/en-US/education/ce334/ce334.pdf |publisher=dentalcare.com |access-date=20 January 2012 |page=12 |year=2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131014172105/http://www.dentalcare.com/media/en-US/education/ce334/ce334.pdf |archive-date=14 October 2013 }}</ref>

==Medical applications==
===Pharmaceuticals===
[[File:Prozac pills.jpg|thumb|alt=large image of just a capsule with words Prozac and DISTA visible|Prozac, one of several notable fluorine-containing drugs]]
Of all commercialized pharmaceutical drugs, twenty percent contain fluorine, including important drugs in many different pharmaceutical classes.<ref>{{cite book |last=Emsley |first=John |title=Nature's building blocks: An A–Z guide to the elements |edition= 2nd |year=2011 |publisher=Oxford University Press | isbn=978-0-19-960563-7 |page=178}}</ref> Fluorine is often added to drug molecules during [[drug design]], as even a single atom can greatly change the chemical properties of the molecule in desirable ways.

Because of the considerable stability of the [[carbon–fluorine bond]], many drugs are fluorinated to delay their [[drug metabolism|metabolism]], which is the chemical process in which the drugs are turned into compounds that allows them to be eliminated. This prolongs their [[half-life|half-lives]] and allows for longer times between dosing and activation. For example, an [[aromatic ring]] may prevent the metabolism of a drug, but this presents a safety problem, because some aromatic compounds are metabolized in the body into poisonous [[epoxide]]s by the organism's native [[enzyme]]s. Substituting a fluorine into a [[Arene substitution patterns|''para'']] position, however, protects the aromatic ring and prevents the epoxide from being produced.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/bk-1985-0283.ch005|title=Polycyclic Hydrocarbons and Carcinogenesis|doi=10.1021/bk-1985-0283.ch005|author1=Stephen S. Hecht|author1-link=Stephen Hecht|author2=Shantu Amin|author3=Assieh A. Melikian|author4=Edmond J. Lavoie|author5=Dietrich Hoffman|date=19 July 1985|isbn=9780841209244|chapter=Chapter 5: Effects of Methyl and Fluorine Substitution on the Metabolic Activation and Tumorigenicity of Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons|pages=85–105}}</ref>

Adding fluorine to biologically active organic compounds increases their [[lipophilicity]] (ability to dissolve in fats), because the carbon–fluorine bond is even more hydrophobic than the [[carbon–hydrogen bond]]. This effect often increases a drug's [[bioavailability]] because of increased cell membrane penetration.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Swinson |first=Joel |journal=PharmaChem |title=Fluorine – A vital element in the medicine chest |year=2005 |pages=26–27 |access-date=26 August 2010 |url=http://www.halocarbon.com/halocarbon_media/swinson_109.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120208080640/http://www.halocarbon.com/halocarbon_media/swinson_109.pdf |archive-date=8 February 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Although the potential of fluorine being released in a fluoride [[leaving group]] depends on its position in the molecule,<ref>{{cite book |title=Pet chemistry: The driving force in molecular imaging |page=144 |publisher=Springer |last=Schubiger |first=P. A. |isbn=9783540326236 |year=2006}}</ref> organofluorides are generally very stable, since the carbon–fluorine bond is strong.

Fluorines also find their uses in common [[mineralocorticoid]]s, a class of drugs that increase the [[blood pressure]]. Adding a fluorine increases both its medical power and anti-inflammatory effects.<ref>{{cite book|title=Glucocorticoids|author1=Goulding, Nicolas J. |author2=Flower, Rod J. |page=40|publisher=Springer|year=2001|isbn=9783764360597}}</ref> Fluorine-containing [[fludrocortisone]] is one of the most common of these drugs.<ref name="dontburn"/> [[Dexamethasone]] and [[triamcinolone]], which are among the most potent of the related synthetic [[corticosteroid]] class of drugs, contain fluorine as well.<ref name="dontburn">{{cite book |title=Pain-relieving procedures: The illustrated guide |page=58 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |year=2012 |last1=Raj |first1=P. Prithvi |last2=Erdine |first2=Serdar |isbn=9781118300459}}</ref>

Several inhaled general [[anesthetic]] agents, including the most commonly used inhaled agents, also contain fluorine. The first fluorinated anesthetic agent, [[halothane]], proved to be much safer (neither explosive nor flammable) and longer-lasting than those previously used. Modern fluorinated anesthetics are longer-lasting still and almost insoluble in blood, which accelerates the awakening.<ref name="anestetics">{{cite book |title=Bioorganic and Medicinal Chemistry of Fluorine |url=https://archive.org/details/bioorganicmedici00bguj |url-access=limited |pages=[https://archive.org/details/bioorganicmedici00bguj/page/n353 335]–336 |publisher= John Wiley & Sons |year=2008 |last1= Bégué |first1=Jean-Pierre |last2=Bonnet-Delpon |first2=Daniele |isbn=9780470281871}}</ref> Examples include [[sevoflurane]], [[desflurane]], [[enflurane]], and [[isoflurane]], all [[hydrofluorocarbon]] derivatives.<ref name="fut">{{cite journal|last1=Filler |first1=R. |last2=Saha |first2=R. |url=http://www.future-science-group.com/_img/pics/fluorine_in_medicinal_chemistry.....pdf |title=Fluorine in medicinal chemistry: A century of progress and a 60-year retrospective of selected highlights |journal=[[Future Medicinal Chemistry]] |volume=1 |issue=5 |pages=777–791 |year=2009 |pmid=21426080 |doi=10.4155/fmc.09.65 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131022021207/http://www.future-science-group.com/_img/pics/fluorine_in_medicinal_chemistry.....pdf |archive-date=2013-10-22 }}</ref>

Prior to the 1980s, [[antidepressant]]s altered not only [[serotonin]] uptake but also the uptake of altered [[norepinephrine]]; the latter caused most of the side effects of antidepressants. The first drug to alter only the serotonin uptake was [[Prozac]]; it gave birth to the extensive [[selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor]] (SSRI) antidepressant class and is the best-selling antidepressant. Many other SSRI antidepressants are fluorinated organics, including [[citalopram|Celexa]], [[Fluvoxamine|Luvox]], and [[escitalopram|Lexapro]].<ref>{{cite book|title = Antidepressants|year = 2004|pages=37–39|last1 = Mitchell|first1 = E. Siobhan|last2 = Triggle|first2 = D. J.|publisher = Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-0192-7}}</ref> [[Quinolone antibiotic|Fluoroquinolones]] are a commonly used family of [[broad-spectrum antibiotic]]s.<ref name="pmid17342653">{{Cite journal|author1=Nelson, J. M. |author2=Chiller, T. M. |author3=Powers, J. H. |author4=Angulo, F. J. |title=Fluoroquinolone-resistant Campylobacter species and the withdrawal of fluoroquinolones from use in poultry: a public health success story |url=https://www.cdc.gov/narms/pdf/JNelson_FluoroquinoloneRCampy_CID.pdf|journal=Clinical Infectious Diseases |volume=44 |issue=7 |pages=977–980 |year=2007 |pmid=17342653 |doi=10.1086/512369|doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Scanning===
{{main|Positron emission tomography|Fludeoxyglucose (18F)}}
[[File:PET scan-normal brain-alzheimers disease brain.PNG|thumb|right|upright=1.5|PET scan for diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease]]
Compounds containing fluorine-18, a radioactive isotope that emits [[positron]]s, are often used in [[positron emission tomography]] (PET) scanning, because the isotope's half-life of about 110 minutes is usefully long by positron-emitter standards. One such [[radiopharmaceutical]] is [[fluorodeoxyglucose|2-deoxy-2-(<sup>18</sup>F)fluoro-D-glucose]] (generically referred to as fludeoxyglucose), commonly abbreviated as <sup>18</sup>F-FDG, or simply FDG.<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1097/00002517-200012000-00016 |last1 = Schmitz |pmid = 11132989 |first1 = A. |year = 2000 |pages = 541–544 |issue = 6 |last2 = Kälicke |volume = 13 |journal= Journal of Spinal Disorders |first2 = T. |last3 = Willkomm |first3 = P. |last4 = Grünwald |first4 = F. |last5 = Kandyba |first5 = J. |last6 = Schmitt |first6 = O.|title=Use of fluorine-18 fluoro-2-deoxy-D-glucose positron emission tomography in assessing the process of tuberculous spondylitis|url=http://www.ecios.org/Synapse/Data/PDFData/0157CIOS/cios-2-167.pdf}}</ref> In PET imaging, FDG can be used for assessing glucose metabolism in the brain and for imaging cancer tumors. After injection into the blood, FDG is taken up by "FDG-avid" tissues with a high need for glucose, such as the brain and most types of malignant tumors.<ref>{{cite journal|title=High aerobic glycolysis of rat hepatoma cells in culture: Role of mitochondrial hexokinase|first1= Ernesto|last1 =Bustamante| first2= Peter L.|last2 =Pedersen|volume = 74|issue = 9|pages = 3735–3739|journal= Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |year=1977|pmid=198801|pmc=431708|doi=10.1073/pnas.74.9.3735|bibcode = 1977PNAS...74.3735B|doi-access= free}}</ref> [[Tomography]], often [[computed tomography|assisted by a computer]] to form a PET/CT (CT stands for "computer tomography") machine, can then be used to diagnose or monitor treatment of cancers, especially [[Hodgkin's lymphoma]], lung cancer, and breast cancer.<ref>{{cite book|title=Cancer imaging: Lung and breast carcinomas|publisher=Academic Press|page=41|author=Hayat, M. A.|year=2007|isbn=9780123742124}}</ref>

Natural fluorine is monoisotopic, consisting solely of [[fluorine-19]]. Fluorine compounds are highly amenable to [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] (NMR), because fluorine-19 has a [[nuclear spin]] of {{frac|1|2}}, a high [[nuclear magnetic moment]], and a high [[magnetogyric ratio]]. Fluorine compounds typically have a fast NMR [[relaxation (NMR)|relaxation]], which enables the use of fast averaging to obtain a [[signal-to-noise ratio]] similar to [[hydrogen atom|hydrogen-1]] NMR spectra.<ref>{{cite book|title = Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy|first = J. H.|last = Nelson|publisher = Prentice Hall|year = 2003|url = https://books.google.com/books?id=czwvAQAAIAAJ|isbn = 978-0-13-033451-0|pages=129–139}}</ref> Fluorine-19 is commonly used in NMR study of metabolism, protein structures and conformational changes.<ref>{{cite journal|doi =10.1146/annurev.bb.25.060196.001115|title = Use of <sup>19</sup>F NMR to probe protein structure and conformational changes|first1 = Mark A.|last1 = Danielson|first2 = Joseph J.|last2 = Falke|year =1996|journal=Annual Review of Biophysics and Biomolecular Structure|volume =25|pages =163–195|pmid =8800468|pmc =2899692}}</ref> In addition, inert fluorinated gases have the potential to be a cheap and efficient tool for imaging lung ventilation.<ref>{{cite journal|doi= 10.1002/mrm.1910390114|title = Imaging lungs using inert fluorinated gases|first1 = Dean O.|last1 = Kuethe|first2 = Arvind|last2 = Caprihan|first3 = Eiichi|last3 = Fukushima|first4 = R. Allen|last4 = Waggoner|year =2005|journal=Magnetic Resonance in Medicine|volume =39|pages =85–88|pmid= 9438441|issue= 1|s2cid = 35741393}}</ref>

===Oxygen transport research===
{{see also|Blood substitute|Liquid breathing}}
Liquid [[fluorocarbon]]s have a very high capacity for holding gas in solution. They can hold more oxygen or carbon dioxide than blood does. For that reason, they have attracted ongoing interest related to the possibility of artificial blood or of liquid breathing.<ref name="Gabrielet">{{cite journal|author1=Gabriel, J. L. |author2=Miller, T. F. |author3=Wolfson, M. R. Jr |author4=Shaffer, T. H. |title= Quantitative structure-activity relationships of perfluorinated hetro-hydrocarbons as potential respiratory media. Application to oxygen solubility, partition coefficient, viscosity, vapor pressure, and density|issue=6|volume=42|pages=968–973|year=1996|journal=ASAIO Journal|doi=10.1097/00002480-199642060-00009|pmid=8959271|s2cid=31161098 }}</ref>

[[File:Perflubron and gentamicin molecules.png|thumb|Computer-generated model of nanocrystal of perflubron (red) and gentamicin (white, an antibiotic)]]
Blood substitutes are the subject of research because the demand for blood transfusions grows faster than donations. In some scenarios, artificial blood may be more convenient or safe. Because fluorocarbons do not normally mix with water, they must be mixed into emulsions (small droplets of perfluorocarbon suspended in water) in order to be used as blood.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Sarkar | first1 = S. | title = Artificial Blood | doi = 10.4103/0972-5229.43685 | journal = Indian Journal of Critical Care Medicine | volume = 12 | issue = 3 | pages = 140–144 | year = 2008 | pmid = 19742251| pmc =2738310 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="Schimmeyer">{{cite journal|author=Schimmeyer, S.|year=2002|journal=Illumin|volume=5|issue=1|url=http://illumin.usc.edu/article.php?articleID=62|title=The search for a blood substitute|access-date=2 December 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111002044847/http://illumin.usc.edu/article.php/?articleID=62|archive-date=2 October 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref> One such product, [[Oxycyte]], has been through initial clinical trials.<ref>{{cite news| author=Tasker, Fred| date=2008-03-19| url=http://www.miamiherald.com/1057/story/459521.html |title=Miami Herald: Artificial blood goes from science fiction to science fact| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080724055545/http://www.miamiherald.com/1057/story/459521.html |archive-date=24 July 2008| publisher=Miami Herald (at noblood.org) }} [http://www.noblood.org/news-hot-topics-such-hepatitis-c-sars-aids/4407-artificial-blood-goes-science-fiction-science-fact.html Alt URL]</ref><ref>{{cite journal|first=Nicole|last=Davis|year=2006|url=http://www.popsci.com/scitech/article/2006-11/better-blood|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110604181554/http://www.popsci.com/scitech/article/2006-11/better-blood|archive-date=2011-06-04| title=Better than blood|journal=[[Popular Science]]|access-date=30 September 2012}}</ref>

Possible medical uses of liquid breathing (which uses pure perfluorocarbon liquid, not a water emulsion) involve assistance for premature babies or for burn patients (if normal lung function is compromised). Both partial and complete filling of the lungs have been considered, although only the former has undergone any significant tests in humans. Several animal tests have been performed and there have been some human partial liquid ventilation trials.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite journal|author1=Shaffer, T. H. |author2=Wolfson, M. R. |author3=Clark, L. R. |title=State of art review: Liquid ventilation|journal=Pediatric Pulmonology|volume=14|issue=102–109|year= 1992|doi=10.1002/ppul.1950140208|pages=102–9|pmid=1437347|s2cid=222167378 }}</ref> One effort, by Alliance Pharmaceuticals, reached clinical trials but was abandoned because of insufficient advantage compared to other therapies.<ref name="Alliance stock drop">{{Cite journal | last1 = Kacmarek | first1 = R. M. | last2 = Wiedemann | first2 = H. P. | last3 = Lavin | first3 = P. T. | last4 = Wedel | first4 = M. K. | last5 = Tütüncü | first5 = A. S. | last6 = Slutsky | first6 = A. S. | title = Partial Liquid Ventilation in Adult Patients with Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome | doi = 10.1164/rccm.200508-1196OC | journal = American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine | volume = 173 | issue = 8 | pages = 882–889 | year = 2006 | pmid = 16254269}}</ref>

Nanocrystals represent a possible method of delivering water- or fat-soluble drugs within a perfluorochemical fluid. The use of these particles is being developed to help treat babies with damaged lungs.<ref name="neonatal liquid breathing review">{{cite journal|last1=Shaffer|first1=Thomas H.|last2=Wolfson|first2=Marla R.|last3=Greenspan|first3=Jay S.|title=Liquid ventilation: Current status|journal=Pediatrics in Review|year=1999|volume=20|issue=12|pages=e134–e142|url=http://pedsinreview.aappublications.org/content/20/12/e134.full|pmid=10587539|doi=10.1542/pir.20-12-e134|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Perfluorocarbons are banned from sports, where they may be used to increase oxygen use for endurance athletes. One cyclist, [[Mauro Gianetti]], was investigated after a near-fatality where PFC use was suspected.<ref>{{cite news|last=Gains|first=Paul|title=A New Threat in Blood Doping|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/10/18/sports/a-new-threat-in-blood-doping.html|newspaper=New York Times|date=October 18, 1998}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.salon.com/1999/04/21/cycling/ | title=Dying to ride| date=1999-04-21}}</ref> Other posited applications include deep-sea diving and space travel, applications that both require total, not partial, liquid ventilation.<ref name=kylstra>{{cite book |title=The feasibility of liquid breathing in man |author=Kylstra, J. A. |year=1977 |publisher=Duke University |url=http://archive.rubicon-foundation.org/4257 |access-date=5 May 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080707005721/http://archive.rubicon-foundation.org/4257 |archive-date=7 July 2008 |url-status=usurped }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.experiencefestival.com/liquid_breathing_-_space_travel |title=Liquid breathing – Space travel |access-date=17 May 2008 |publisher=experiencefestival.com |author=The Global Oneness Commitment |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100417124924/http://www.experiencefestival.com/liquid_breathing_-_space_travel |archive-date=17 April 2010 }}</ref> The 1989 film ''[[The Abyss]]'' depicted a fictional use of perfluorocarbon for human diving but also filmed a real rat surviving while cooled and immersed in perfluorocarbon.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Aljean Harmetz|year=1989|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/08/06/movies/film-the-abyss-a-foray-into-deep-waters.html|title= FILM; 'The Abyss': A foray into deep waters |journal=The New York Times|access-date=2 October 2012}}</ref> (See also [[Liquid breathing#Examples in fiction|list of fictional treatments]] of perfluorocarbon breathing.)

==Agrichemicals==
An estimated 30% of [[agrochemical|agrichemical compounds]] contain fluorine.<ref>{{cite web|title = Fluorine's treasure trove|access-date=20 February 2011|url = http://www.icis.com/Articles/2006/09/30/2016413/fluorines-treasure-trove.html|publisher = ICIS news|date = 2006-10-02}}</ref> Most of them are used as poisons, but a few stimulate growth instead. 
[[Image:1080PoisonWarning gobeirne.png|thumb|Sign warning of poisonous sodium fluoroacetate baits]]

[[Sodium fluoroacetate]] has been used as an insecticide, but it is especially effective against mammalian pests.<ref>{{cite report|url=https://www.pwrc.usgs.gov/infobase/eisler/CHR_30_Sodium_monofluoroacetate.pdf |last=Eisler |first=Ronald |title=Biological report 27: Sodium monofluoroacetate (1080) Hazards to fish, wildlife and invertebrates: A synoptic review |publisher=Patuxent Environmental Science Center (U.S. National Biological Service) |year=1995 |access-date=5 June 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100612141525/http://www.pwrc.usgs.gov/infobase/eisler/CHR_30_Sodium_monofluoroacetate.pdf |archive-date=12 June 2010 }}</ref> The name "1080" refers to the catalogue number of the poison, which became its brand name.<ref name="Proudfoot"/> Fluoroacetate is similar to acetate, which has a pivotal role in the [[Krebs cycle]] (a key part of cell metabolism). Fluoroacetate halts the cycle and causes cells to be deprived of energy.<ref name="Proudfoot"/> Several other insecticides contain sodium fluoride, which is much less toxic than fluoroacetate.<ref>{{cite web|publisher = Scorecard|title = Class I ozone-depleting substances|work = Sodium fluoride – pesticidal uses|url = http://scorecard.goodguide.com/chemical-profiles/pesticides.tcl?edf_substance_id=7681-49-4|access-date = 20 February 2011|archive-date = 11 July 2011|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110711111636/http://scorecard.goodguide.com/chemical-profiles/pesticides.tcl?edf_substance_id=7681-49-4|url-status = usurped}}</ref> Insects fed 29-fluorostigmasterol use it to produce fluoroacetates. If a fluorine is transferred to a body cell, it blocks metabolism at the position occupied.<ref>{{cite book|pages=1–19|author=Barnette, William E.|year=1995|isbn=9781859570333|publisher=Smithers Rapra Publishing|title=Fluorine in agriculture|chapter=Physical Organic Aspects of Fluorinated Argichemicals}}</ref>

[[Trifluralin]] was widely used in the 20th century, for example, in over half of U.S. cotton field acreage in 1998.<ref name="trifluralin">{{cite journal|journal=Pesticides News|volume=52|year=2001|pages=20–21|title=Fact sheet: Trifluralin}}<!--|Author not stated--></ref> Because of its suspected carcinogenic properties some Northern European countries banned it in 1993.<ref>{{cite report|author = European Commission|title = Trifluralin |year = 2007| url =http://www.unece.org/fileadmin/DAM/env/lrtap/TaskForce/popsxg/2008/Trifluralin_RA%20dossier_proposal%20for%20submission%20to%20the%20UNECE%20POP%20Protocol.pdf}}</ref> As of 2015, the European Union has banned it, although Dow made a case to cancel the decision in 2011.<ref>Case T-475/07, Dow AgroSciences Ltd vs. European Commission (2011). The General Court of European Union (Third Camber).</ref>

==Biochemistry==
[[File:Gifblaar.jpg|thumb|South Africa's [[gifblaar]] is one of the few organisms that naturally produce fluorine compounds]]
Biologically synthesized organofluorines are few in number, although some are widely produced.<ref name=Gribble>{{cite book|last1 =Gribble|first1 =Gordon W.|title =Organofluorines|chapter =Naturally occurring organofluorines|volume =3N|pages =121–136|year =2002|doi =10.1007/10721878_5|series =The Handbook of Environmental Chemistry|isbn =978-3-540-42064-4}}</ref><ref name="Murphy2003">{{Cite journal| last1 = Murphy |pmid=12738270| first1 = C.| last2 = Schaffrath| first2 = C.| last3 = O'Hagan| first3 = D.| title = Fluorinated natural products: The biosynthesis of fluoroacetate and 4-fluorothreonine in ''Streptomyces cattleya''| doi = 10.1016/S0045-6535(03)00191-7| year = 2003| journal= Chemosphere| volume = 52| issue = 2| pages =455–461|bibcode=2003Chmsp..52..455M}}</ref> The most common example is [[sodium fluoroacetate|fluoroacetate]], with an active poison molecule identical to commercial "1080". It is used as a [[plant defense against herbivores|defense against herbivores]] by at least 40 green plants in Australia, Brazil, and Africa;<ref name="Proudfoot">{{cite journal |last1=Proudfoot|first1 = A. T.|last2= Bradberry|first2= S. M. |last3= Vale |first3= J. A. |title=Sodium fluoroacetate poisoning |journal=Toxicological Reviews |volume=25 |issue=4 |pages=213–219 |year=2006 |pmid=17288493 |doi=10.2165/00139709-200625040-00002|s2cid = 29189551}}</ref> other biologically synthesized organofluorines include ω-fluoro [[fatty acid]]s, [[fluoroacetone]], and 2-fluorocitrate.<ref name="Murphy2003"/> In bacteria, the enzyme [[adenosyl-fluoride synthase]], which makes the carbon–fluorine bond, has been isolated. The discovery was touted as possibly leading to biological routes for organofluorine synthesis.<ref>{{cite journal|last1= O'Hagan |first1=D.|last2= Schaffrath |first2=C. |last3=Cobb |first3=S. L. |last4=Hamilton |first4=J. T. |last5=Murphy |first5=C. D.|year = 2002|title = Biochemistry: Biosynthesis of an organofluorine molecule|journal= Nature |volume = 416|page = 279 |pmid = 11907567|doi = 10.1038/416279a|issue = 6878|bibcode = 2002Natur.416..279O |doi-access= free }}</ref>

Fluoride is considered a semi-essential element for humans: not necessary to sustain life, but contributing (within narrow limits of daily intake) to dental health and bone strength. Daily requirements for fluorine in humans vary with age and sex, ranging from 0.01 mg in infants below 6 months to 4 mg in adult males, with an upper tolerable limit of 0.7 mg in infants to 10 mg in adult males and females.<ref name="quott">{{cite report|last1=Olivares |first1=M. |last2=Uauy |first2=R. |year=2004 |url=https://www.who.int/water_sanitation_health/dwq/en/nutoverview.pdf |title=Essential nutrients in drinking water: Tables 2,6,7,8. (Draft) |publisher=[[World Health Organization|WHO]] |access-date=30 December 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121019174633/http://www.who.int/water_sanitation_health/dwq/en/nutoverview.pdf |archive-date=19 October 2012 }}</ref><ref>
Food and Nutrition Board, Institute of Medicine, National Academies. Dietary Reference Intakes (DRIs): Recommended Dietary Allowances and Adequate Intakes, Elements.
 http://www.nationalacademies.org/hmd/~/media/Files/Activity%20Files/Nutrition/DRI-Tables/2_%20RDA%20and%20AI%20Values_Vitamin%20and%20Elements.pdf?la=en {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181113060244/http://www.nationalacademies.org/hmd/~/media/Files/Activity%20Files/Nutrition/DRI-Tables/2_%20RDA%20and%20AI%20Values_Vitamin%20and%20Elements.pdf?la=en |date=2018-11-13 }} Accessed Jan 2 2019.
</ref> Small amounts of fluoride may be beneficial for bone strength, but this is an issue only in the formulation of artificial diets.<ref name="gastroenterology1">{{cite journal|last1 = Nielsen|first1 = Forrest H.|doi = 10.1053/j.gastro.2009.07.072|title = Micronutrients in parenteral nutrition: Boron, silicon, and fluoride|pmid = 19874950|year = 2009|journal = Gastroenterology|volume = 137|issue = 5 Suppl|pages = S55–S60|doi-access = free}}</ref> (See also [[fluoride deficiency]].)

==Hazards==
{{NFPA 704|Health = 4|Flammability = 0|Reactivity = 4|S= W|caption=The fire diamond hazard sign for elemental fluorine.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://cameochemicals.noaa.gov/chemical/764 | title=FLUORINE | CAMEO Chemicals | NOAA}}</ref>}}
[[File:DOT hazmat signs - Fluorine.svg|thumb|right|upright=1.6|alt=4 diagonal placards with warnings, poison, corrosive, inhalant, oxidant|The U.S. hazard signs for commercially transported fluorine<ref name="NOAA data sheet">[[#NOAASheet|NOAA <sub>9</sub>F data sheet]].</ref>]]

===Fluorine gas===
Elemental fluorine is highly toxic. Above a concentration of 25 ppm, it causes significant irritation while attacking the eyes, airways and lungs and affecting the liver and kidneys. At a concentration of 100 ppm, human eyes and noses are seriously damaged.<ref>{{harvnb|Keplinger|Suissa|1968}}.</ref> People can be exposed to fluorine in the workplace by breathing it in, skin contact, or eye contact. The [[Occupational Safety and Health Administration]] (OSHA) has set the legal limit ([[Permissible exposure limit]]) for fluorine exposure in the workplace as 0.1 ppm (0.2 mg/m<sup>3</sup>) over an 8-hour workday. The [[National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health]] (NIOSH) has set a [[recommended exposure limit]] (REL) of 0.1 ppm (0.2 mg/m<sup>3</sup>) over an 8-hour workday. At levels of 25 ppm, fluorine is [[IDLH|immediately dangerous to life and health]].<ref>{{Cite web|title = CDC - NIOSH Pocket Guide to Chemical Hazards - Fluorine|url = https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0289.html|website = www.cdc.gov|access-date= 2015-11-03}}</ref>

===Hydrofluoric acid===
{{See also|Chemical burn}}
[[File:HF burned hands.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|alt=left and right hands, two views, burned index fingers|Typical HF burns: the outward signs may not be evident for 24 hours, after which calcium treatments are less effective.<ref name=Eaton>{{cite web|last=Eaton|first=Charles|title=Figure hfl|url=http://www.eatonhand.com/complic/figures/hfl.htm|work=E-Hand.com: the electronic textbook of hand surgery|publisher=The Hand Center (former practice of Dr. Eaton)|access-date=28 September 2013}}</ref>]]
[[Hydrofluoric acid]], the water solution of hydrogen fluoride (HF), is a contact poison. Even though it is from a chemical perspective a relatively weak acid, it is far more dangerous than conventional strong [[mineral acids]], such as [[nitric acid]], [[sulfuric acid]], or [[hydrochloric acid]]. Owing to its lesser chemical dissociation in water (remaining a neutral molecule), hydrogen fluoride penetrates tissue more quickly than typical acids. Poisoning can occur readily through the skin or eyes or when inhaled or swallowed. From 1984 to 1994, at least nine workers died in the United States from accidents with HF.<ref name="OSHA"/>

Once in the blood, hydrogen fluoride reacts with calcium and magnesium, resulting in electrolyte imbalances, potentially including [[hypocalcemia]]. The consequent effect on the heart ([[cardiac arrhythmia]]) may be fatal.<ref name="OSHA">{{harvnb|Blodgett|Suruda|Crouch|2001}}.</ref> Formation of insoluble [[calcium fluoride]] also causes severe pain.<ref name=Goldfrank>{{Harvnb|Hoffman et al.|2007|p=1333}}.</ref> Burns with areas larger than 160 cm<sup>2</sup>, about the size of a man's hand, can cause serious systemic toxicity.<ref name='RMTHFE'>{{Harvnb|HSM|2006}}.</ref>

Symptoms of exposure to hydrofluoric acid may not be immediately evident, with an eight-hour delay for 50% HF and up to 24 hours for lower concentrations. Hydrogen fluoride interferes with nerve function, meaning that burns may not initially be painful. If the burn has been initially noticed, then HF should be washed off with a forceful stream of water for ten to fifteen minutes to prevent its further penetration into the body. Clothing used by the person burned may also present a danger.<ref>{{harvnb|Fischman|2001|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=PyUSgdZUGr4C&pg=PA458 458–459]}}.</ref> Hydrofluoric acid exposure is often treated with [[calcium gluconate]], a source of Ca<sup>2+</sup> that binds with the fluoride ions. Skin burns can be treated with a water wash and 2.5 percent calcium gluconate gel<ref name="pmid2741315">{{harvnb|El Saadi et al.|1989}}.</ref><ref name="pmid17091088">{{harvnb|Roblin et al.|2006}}.</ref> or special rinsing solutions.<ref name="pmid15461243">{{harvnb|Hultén et al.|2004}}.</ref> Because HF is absorbed, further medical treatment is necessary. Calcium gluconate may be injected or administered intravenously. Use of [[calcium chloride]] is contraindicated and may lead to severe complications. Sometimes surgical excision of tissue or amputation is required.<ref name="RMTHFE"/><ref>{{Harvnb|Zorich|1991|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=sdB3KjhWzFQC&pg=PA183 182–3]}}.</ref>

===Fluoride ion===
[[File:Fluworôze egzostozes1-800h.jpg|thumb|right|upright|alt=knobby hoofed leg|Moroccan cow with fluorosis, from industrial contamination]]
{{See also|Fluoride toxicity}}
Soluble fluorides are moderately toxic. For sodium fluoride, the lethal dose for adults is 5–10 g, which is equivalent to 32–64 mg of elemental fluoride per kilogram of body weight.<ref name="zzzzzzz23">{{Harvnb|Liteplo et al.|2002|p=100}}.</ref> The dose that may lead to adverse health effects is about one fifth of the lethal dose.<ref name="Nochimson"/> Chronic excess fluoride consumption can lead to [[skeletal fluorosis]], a disease of the bones that affects millions in Asia and Africa.<ref name="Nochimson"/><ref name="pmid19305069">{{harvnb|Reddy|2009}}.</ref>

The fluoride ion is readily absorbed by the stomach and intestines. Ingested fluoride forms hydrofluoric acid in the stomach. In this form, fluoride crosses cell membranes and then binds with calcium and interferes with various enzymes. Fluoride is [[excretion|excreted]] through urine. Fluoride exposure limits are based on urine testing, which is used to determine the human body's capacity for ridding itself of fluoride.<ref name="Nochimson">{{Harvnb|Shin|Silverberg|2013}}.</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Baez|Baez|Marthaler|2000}}.</ref>

Historically, most cases of fluoride poisoning have been caused by accidental ingestion of insecticides containing inorganic fluoride.<ref>{{Harvnb|Augenstein et al.|1991}}.</ref> Most calls to poison control centers for possible fluoride poisoning come from the ingestion of fluoride-containing toothpaste.<ref name="Nochimson"/> Malfunction of water fluoridation equipment has occurred several times, including an Alaskan incident that sickened nearly 300 people and killed one.<ref name=Gessner94>{{harvnb|Gessner et al.|1994}}.</ref>

===Biopersistence===
{{main|Perfluorinated compound}}
Because of the strength of the carbon–fluorine bond, organofluorines endure in the environment. [[Perfluorinated compound]]s (PFCs) have attracted particular attention as [[persistent organic pollutant|persistent global contaminants]].  These compounds can enter the environment from their direct uses in waterproofing treatments and firefighting foams or indirectly from leaks from fluoropolymer production plants (where they are intermediates). Because of the acid group, PFCs are water-soluble in low concentrations.<ref name=Giesy>{{Cite journal | doi=10.1021/es022253t|pmid = 11999053|title = Peer Reviewed: Perfluorochemical Surfactants in the Environment| journal=Environmental Science & Technology| volume=36| issue=7| pages=146A–152A|year = 2002|last1 = Giesy|first1 = John P.| last2=Kannan| first2=Kurunthachalam|bibcode = 2002EnST...36..146G| doi-access=free}}</ref>  While there are other PFAAs, the lion's share of environmental research has been done on the two most well-known: [[perfluorooctanesulfonic acid]] (PFOS) and [[perfluorooctanoic acid]] (PFOA).  The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency classifies these materials as "emerging contaminants" based on the growing but still incomplete understanding of their environmental impact.<ref name="PFOA">{{cite journal |vauthors=Steenland K, Fletcher T, Savitz DA |title=Epidemiologic evidence on the health effects of perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) |journal=Environ. Health Perspect. |volume=118 |issue=8 |pages=1100–8 |year=2010 |pmid=20423814 |pmc=2920088 |doi=10.1289/ehp.0901827 |bibcode=2010EnvHP.118.1100S }}</ref><ref name="PFOA evidence"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.epa.gov/fedfac/pdf/emerging_contaminants_pfos_pfoa.pdf|title=Emerging Contaminants Fact Sheet- PFOS and PFOA|access-date=November 1, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029202537/http://www.epa.gov/fedfac/pdf/emerging_contaminants_pfos_pfoa.pdf |archive-date=October 29, 2013 |date=2013-04-23}}</ref>

Trace quantities of PFCs have been detected worldwide, in organisms from polar bears in the Arctic to the global human population.  Both PFOS and PFOA have been detected in breast milk and the blood of newborns.  A 2013 review showed widely varying amounts of PFOS and PFOA in different soils and groundwater, with no clear pattern of one chemical dominating. PFC concentrations were generally higher in areas with more human population or industrial activity, and areas with more PFOS generally also had more PFOA.<ref>P. Zareitalabad, J. Siemens, M. Hamer, W. Amelung [http://safeguard.giqs.org/fileadmin/web_safeguard/content/Berichte_Protokolle2009/Schlussdokumente/CHEM13643.pdf Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) in surface waters, sediments, soils and wastewater – A review on concentrations and distribution coefficients] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304070053/http://safeguard.giqs.org/fileadmin/web_safeguard/content/Berichte_Protokolle2009/Schlussdokumente/CHEM13643.pdf |date=2016-03-04 }} Chemosphere 91 (2013) 725–732. Review</ref>  the two chemicals have been found at different concentrations in different populations; for example, one study showed more PFOS than PFOA in Germans, while another study showed the reverse for Americans. PFCs may be starting to decrease in the biosphere: one study indicated that PFOS levels in wildlife in Minnesota were decreasing, presumably because [[3M]] discontinued its production.<ref name="PFOA"/><ref name="PFOA evidence"/>

[[File:PFOS-3D-vdW.png|The PFOS molecule|thumb]]
In the body, PFCs bind to proteins such as [[serum albumin]]. Their tissue distribution in humans is unknown, but studies in rats suggest it is present mostly in the liver, kidney, and blood. They are not metabolized by the body but are excreted by the kidneys. Dwell time in the body varies greatly by species.  Rodents have half-lives of days, while in humans they remain for years. Many animals show sex differences in the ability to rid the body of PFAAs, but without a clear pattern. Gender differences of half lives vary by animal species.<ref name="PFOA"/><ref name="PFOA evidence"/><ref name="tox">{{cite journal |last1=Lau |first1=Christopher |last2=Anitole |first2=Katherine |last3=Hodes |first3=Colette |last4=Lai |first4=David |last5=Pfahles-Hutchens |first5=Andrea |last6=Seed |first6=Jennifer |title=Perfluoroalkyl Acids: A Review of Monitoring and Toxicological Findings |journal=Toxicological Sciences |date=October 2007 |volume=99 |issue=2 |pages=366–394 |doi=10.1093/toxsci/kfm128 |pmid=17519394 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

The potential health impact of PFCs is unclear. Unlike chlorinated hydrocarbons, PFCs are not [[lipophilic]] (stored in fat), nor [[Genotoxicity|genotoxic]] (damaging genes). Both PFOA and PFOS in high doses cause cancer and the death of newborns in rodents. Studies on humans have not been able to prove an impact at current exposures. [[Bottlenose dolphin]]s have some of the highest PFOS concentrations of any wildlife studied; one study suggests an impact on their immune systems.<ref name="PFOA"/><ref name="PFOA evidence">{{cite journal|pmc=2072861|date=November 2007|last1=Betts|first1=Kellyn|title=PFOS and PFOA in Humans: New Study Links Prenatal Exposure to Lower Birth Weight|journal=Environmental Health Perspectives|volume=115|issue=11|page=A550|pmid=18007977|doi=10.1289/ehp.115-a550a}}</ref><ref name="tox"/>

The biochemical causes of toxicity are also unclear and may differ by molecule, health effect, and even animal. [[PPAR-alpha]] is a protein that interacts with PFAAs and is commonly implicated in contaminant-caused rodent cancers.<ref name="PFOA"/><ref name="PFOA evidence"/><ref name="tox"/>

Less fluorinated chemicals (i.e. not perfluorinated compounds) can also be detected in the environment. Because biological systems do not metabolize fluorinated molecules easily, fluorinated pharmaceuticals like antibiotics and antidepressants can be found in treated city sewage and wastewater.<ref>{{Harvnb|Lietz|Meyer|2006|pp=7–8}}.</ref> Fluorine-containing agrichemicals are measurable in farmland [[Surface runoff|runoff]] and nearby rivers.<ref>{{harvnb|Ahrens|2011}}.</ref>

extract:
Fluorine may interact with biological systems in the form of fluorine-containing compounds. Though elemental fluorine (F2) is very rare in everyday life, fluorine-containing compounds such as fluorite occur naturally as minerals. Naturally occurring organofluorine compounds are extremely rare. Man-made fluoride compounds are common and are used in medicines, pesticides, and materials. Twenty percent of all commercialized pharmaceuticals contain fluorine, including Lipitor and Prozac. In many contexts, fluorine-containing compounds are harmless or even beneficial to living organisms; in others, they are toxic.
Aside from their use in medicine, man-made fluorinated compounds have also played a role in several noteworthy environmental concerns. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), once major components of numerous commercial aerosol products, have proven damaging to Earth's ozone layer and resulted in the wide-reaching Montreal Protocol; though in truth the chlorine in CFCs is the destructive actor, fluorine is an important part of these molecules because it makes them very stable and long-lived. Similarly, the stability of many organofluorine compounds has raised the issue of biopersistence. Long-lived molecules from waterproofing sprays, for example PFOA and PFOS, are found worldwide in the tissues of wildlife and humans, including newborn children.
Fluorine biology is also relevant to a number of cutting-edge technologies. PFCs (perfluorocarbons) are capable of holding enough oxygen to support human liquid breathing. Organofluorine in the form of its radioisotope 18F is also at the heart of a modern medical imaging technique known as positron emission tomography (PET). A PET scan produces three-dimensional colored images of parts of the body that use a lot of sugar, particularly the brain or tumors.
